The wavelength at which a body radiates most is fixed by its **temperature** alone -
Wien's displacement law.
**Step 1 — state the law.**
**λ_max T = b = 2·9 x 10⁻³ m K** ✓
so the peak wavelength depends **only** on the absolute temperature.
**Step 2 — see what the other factors do.**
the **nature** of the surface affects the **emissivity**, hence how much is radiated,
but not where the peak lies ✓
the **area** affects the **total** power, P = σAT⁴, again not the wavelength ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** The wavelength depends on the **temperature of the surface** ✓
**Worked values.**
a body at **300 K**: λ_max = 2·9 x 10⁻³/300 = **9·7 µm**, in the infrared ✓ which is
why thermal cameras work at that wavelength
the **Sun** at 5800 K: λ_max = **500 nm**, in the green - the middle of the visible
range ✓
a filament at 3000 K: **970 nm**, just into the infrared, which is why an incandescent
lamp wastes most of its energy as heat.
**Why the peak shifts to shorter wavelengths as things get hotter.** Heat a poker and
it glows first **dull red**, then **orange**, then **yellow-white** ✓ The whole
spectrum brightens, but its peak marches towards the blue.
**How astronomers use it.** Measuring a star's colour gives its surface temperature
directly ✓ Betelgeuse at 3500 K is red, the Sun at 5800 K yellow, Rigel at 11000 K
blue-white.
**The companion law.** **Stefan's law**, P = σAT⁴, gives the **total** power ✓ Wien
tells you **what colour**, Stefan **how much**. Together they describe thermal radiation
completely.
**Where the surface's nature does enter.** Through the **emissivity** ε in
P = εσAT⁴ ✓ A dull black surface has ε near 1, polished silver near 0·02 - so they
radiate very different amounts, but at the same temperature their spectra peak at the
**same** wavelength.
**Why "all of the above" is wrong.** It is tempting, since each factor does affect
radiation **somehow** ✓ But the question asks specifically about the **wavelength**,
and only temperature determines that.
∴ the temperature of the surface.

Rearrange Stefan's law and read off the units.
**Step 1 — write the law.**
**E = σT⁴** ✓
with E the power radiated **per unit area**.
**Step 2 — solve for σ.**
σ = E/T⁴ ✓
**Step 3 — substitute the units.**
E is in **W m⁻²** and T⁴ in **K⁴**, so
σ is in **W m⁻² K⁻⁴** ✓
**The numerical value.**
σ = **5·67 x 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴** ✓
**Why the fourth power.** It follows from integrating Planck's radiation law over all
wavelengths ✓ Stefan found it experimentally in 1879 and Boltzmann derived it
thermodynamically in 1884 - hence the Stefan-Boltzmann law.
**How dramatic the dependence is.** Doubling the absolute temperature multiplies the
radiated power **sixteenfold** ✓ which is why a filament at 3000 K is so much brighter
than one at 1500 K, and why a small temperature rise in a star transforms its
luminosity.
**A worked instance.** A black body of 1 m² at 300 K radiates
E = (5·67 x 10⁻⁸)(300)⁴ = **459 W** ✓
and at 600 K, **7348 W** - sixteen times as much.
**The full form for a real body.**
P = **εσA T⁴** ✓
with ε the emissivity, 1 for a perfect black body and less for anything else.
**The net exchange with surroundings.**
P_net = εσA(T⁴ − T₀⁴) ✓
which for small differences reduces to Newton's law of cooling, P ∝ (T − T₀).
**Why the kelvin scale is essential.** The law uses **absolute** temperature ✓ Using
celsius would give nonsense - a body at 0 °C would radiate nothing, and one below zero
would radiate negatively.
**The dimensional formula.**
[σ] = [M T⁻³ K⁻⁴] ✓ since W m⁻² = kg s⁻³.
**Reading the distractors.** **W m⁻² K⁻¹** ✗ is the unit of a heat-transfer
coefficient. **W m K⁻⁴** ✗ has the length power wrong, and **N m⁻² K⁴** ✗ is a pressure
times K⁴ ✓ Only W m⁻² K⁻⁴ follows from E/T⁴.
∴ Wm⁻²k⁻⁴.

Use the constant-pressure heat to find C_p, then **C_v = C_p − R**.
**Step 1 — find C_p from the given data.**
Q_p = n C_p ΔT
310 = (2)(C_p)(10)
**C_p = 15·5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹** ✓
**Step 2 — apply Mayer's relation.**
C_p − C_v = R
C_v = 15·5 − 8·31
= **7·19 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹** ✓
**Step 3 — find the heat at constant volume.**
Q_v = n C_v ΔT
= (2)(7·19)(10)
= **143·8 ≈ 144 J** ✓
**Why less heat is needed at constant volume.** At constant **pressure** the gas
**expands** and does work on its surroundings ✓ That work must be paid for by extra
heat. At constant **volume** no work is done, and every joule goes into internal
energy.
**The work done in the constant-pressure case.**
W = nRΔT = (2)(8·31)(10) = **166 J** ✓
and indeed 310 − 166 = **144 J** ✓ exactly the constant-volume figure - the first law,
Q = ΔU + W, in action.
**Why Mayer's relation takes that form.** For one mole,
ΔU is the same in both processes, since U depends only on T ✓
Q_p = ΔU + RΔT and Q_v = ΔU
subtracting gives **C_p − C_v = R** ✓
**What kind of gas this is.** C_v = 7·19 lies between the monatomic 12·5 and... in fact
**below** the monatomic value of (3/2)R = 12·47 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ ✓ so the data are not those
of any real ideal gas. The question is an exercise in Mayer's relation rather than a
description of a real sample.
**The ratio implied.**
γ = C_p/C_v = 15·5/7·19 = **2·16** ✓ larger than the monatomic 1·67, again showing the
numbers are illustrative.
**Reading the distractors.** **452 J** ✗ and **384 J** ✗ exceed the constant-pressure
heat, which is impossible - constant-volume heating always needs **less**. **276 J** ✗
corresponds to C_v = 13·8, that is C_p − C_v = 1·7, not R ✓
∴ 144 J.

Note: the printed key gives the second option, 276 J. Mayer's relation C_v = C_p − R
with C_p = 15·5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ gives C_v = 7·19 and hence Q_v = 144 J, confirmed by the
first-law check Q_p − W = 310 − 166 = 144 J. The key has been corrected to the third
option.

In the **steady state** the same heat per second passes through both sections.
**Step 1 — write the heat flow through each.** With the same cross-section A and the
junction at temperature T:
through copper: (dQ/dt) = k_c A(100 − T)/18
through steel: (dQ/dt) = k_s A(T − 0)/6 ✓
**Step 2 — equate them.** In the steady state no heat accumulates at the junction:
k_c(100 − T)/18 = k_s T/6 ✓
**Step 3 — substitute k_c = 9k_s.**
9k_s(100 − T)/18 = k_s T/6
(100 − T)/2 = T/6 ✓
**Step 4 — solve.**
6(100 − T) = 2T
600 = 8T
**T = 75 °C** ✓
**Why the junction sits so close to the hot end.** Copper conducts **nine times** better
than steel, so it needs only a small temperature drop to carry the heat ✓ The steel,
being a poor conductor, requires a large drop. Here copper drops **25 °C** and steel
**75 °C**.
**The thermal-resistance view, which is quicker.**
R_th = L/(kA) ✓
copper: 18/(9k_s A) = **2/(k_s A)**
steel: 6/(k_s A) = **6/(k_s A)** ✓
The two resistances are in the ratio **1 : 3**, so the 100 °C divides as 25 : 75 - and
the junction is at **75 °C** ✓ exactly as the algebra gives.
**Why this is like a potential divider.** Heat flow obeys the same mathematics as
current, with temperature difference as the "voltage" ✓ Two resistors in series divide
the voltage in proportion to their resistances - and here the "voltage" is 100 °C.
**Why copper's greater length does not save it.** It is three times longer, but nine
times more conductive ✓ so its thermal resistance is still three times **smaller**.
**A check on the heat flow.** Taking k_s A = 1 in suitable units:
through copper: (100 − 75)/2 = **12·5**
through steel: 75/6 = **12·5** ✓ equal, as the steady state demands.
**Where this matters.** Composite walls, lagged pipes and heat sinks are all analysed
this way ✓ and the rule is that the **poorest** conductor dominates the temperature
drop, which is why a thin layer of insulation is so effective.
∴ 75°C.

Stefan's law makes the radiated power go as **T⁴**, with T in **kelvin**.
**Step 1 — convert both temperatures.**
27 °C = 27 + 273 = **300 K**
627 °C = 627 + 273 = **900 K** ✓
**Step 2 — form the ratio.**
E₂/E₁ = (900/300)⁴
= 3⁴
= **81** ✓
**Step 3 — compute.**
E₂ = 0·5 x 81
= **40·5 J per second** ✓
**Why the kelvin conversion is essential.** Using celsius would give (627/27)⁴ = 290000,
a wildly wrong answer ✓ Stefan's law uses **absolute** temperature, and this is the step
the question is really testing.
**How steep the fourth power is.** Tripling the absolute temperature multiplies the
power **eighty-one fold** ✓ The body is only 600 °C hotter, yet it radiates eighty
times as strongly - which is why a furnace at red heat loses energy so much faster than
a warm room.
**Where the law comes from.**
E = σT⁴ for a black body ✓
derived by integrating Planck's spectrum over all wavelengths, and found experimentally
by Stefan in 1879.
**The accompanying colour shift.** By Wien's law, λ_max = 2·9 x 10⁻³/T:
at 300 K: **9·7 µm**, deep infrared - invisible ✓
at 900 K: **3·2 µm**, still infrared but with enough of a visible tail to glow **dull
red** ✓
Red heat begins at about 800 K.
**Why the area and emissivity do not appear.** They are the **same** body, so both
cancel in the ratio ✓ Only the temperature has changed.
**The net loss to the surroundings.** If the room is at 300 K, the body at 900 K loses
E_net ∝ (900⁴ − 300⁴) = 0·5(81 − 1) = **40 J s⁻¹** ✓ barely less than 40·5, because the
surroundings' contribution is negligible at the higher temperature.
**A sense of scale.** For a black body of 1 m²:
at 300 K: **459 W**
at 900 K: **37·2 kW** ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **162 J** ✗ is 0·5 x 324, using 3⁴ x 4. **13·5 J** ✗ uses
3³, and **135 J** ✗ uses 3⁴ x 10/3 ✓ Only the exact fourth power gives 81.
∴ 40.5 J.

Resistance rises linearly with temperature; work from the **0 °C** reference that α
implies.
**Step 1 — note the reference.** The coefficient α is defined with respect to
**0 °C = 273 K**:
R_t = R₀(1 + αt), with t in degrees celsius ✓
**Step 2 — find R₀ from the given point.** At 300 K, that is **27 °C**:
0·3 = R₀[1 + (1·5 x 10⁻³)(27)]
= R₀(1·0405)
**R₀ = 0·2883 Ω** ✓
**Step 3 — find the temperature at which R = 0·6 Ω.**
0·6 = 0·2883[1 + (1·5 x 10⁻³)t]
2·081 = 1 + 1·5 x 10⁻³ t
1·081 = 1·5 x 10⁻³ t
**t = 721 °C** ✓
**Step 4 — convert to kelvin.**
T = 721 + 273
= **994 ≈ 993 K** ✓
**Why the reference point matters so much.** Taking 300 K itself as the reference would
give ΔT = 1/α = 667 K and T = **967 K** - close, but not one of the options ✓ The
standard definition of α is relative to **0 °C**, and the question's figures are built
on it.
**Why a metal's resistance rises with temperature.** Hotter lattice ions vibrate more
vigorously, so conduction electrons collide more often and the mean free time τ falls ✓
Since ρ = m/(ne²τ), the resistivity rises - and in a metal the carrier density n is
essentially fixed.
**How large α is for common metals.**
copper: **0·0039 K⁻¹**
platinum: **0·0039 K⁻¹**
tungsten: **0·0045 K⁻¹** ✓
The value here, 0·0015, is smaller - characteristic of an alloy such as nichrome, which
is chosen for heating elements precisely because its resistance is stable.
**The practical use of this behaviour.** A **platinum resistance thermometer** measures
temperature from resistance over a huge range, from 14 K to 1200 K ✓ with excellent
reproducibility.
**The contrast with a semiconductor.** There α is **negative** and much larger in
magnitude ✓ so a thermistor's resistance **falls** steeply with temperature.
**Reading the distractors.** **690 K** ✗ and **720 K** ✗ are the celsius answer and its
neighbourhood read as kelvin - the trap for anyone who forgets to add 273. **345 K** ✗
is far too small a rise for a doubling ✓
∴ 993 K.

The same **torque** is needed, so a shorter lever arm demands a larger force.
**Step 1 — state the condition.** To open the door, the moment about the hinges must be
the same:
F₁d₁ = F₂d₂ ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.**
(1)(1·6) = F₂(0·4) ✓
**Step 3 — solve.**
F₂ = 1·6/0·4
= **4 N** ✓
**Why the force must be four times larger.** The distance from the hinge has been cut to
a **quarter** - from 1·6 m to 0·4 m ✓ and torque is force **times** distance, so the
force must rise in exact inverse proportion.
**Why door handles are at the far edge.** To maximise the moment arm ✓ A handle placed
near the hinge would need an impractical force, as this calculation shows. It is the
simplest everyday application of the principle of moments.
**The torque itself.**
τ = **1·6 N m** in both cases ✓ That is the physically meaningful quantity; the force
and the distance are merely two ways of supplying it.
**Why the force must be perpendicular to the door.** The general formula is
τ = Fd sin θ ✓ A push **along** the door, towards the hinge, has θ = 0 and produces no
turning effect at all - which is why pushing on the edge of a door edge-on achieves
nothing.
**The same principle elsewhere.** Spanners are made long, nutcrackers have long handles,
and a crowbar works by exactly this trade of distance for force ✓ In each case the
**work** done is the same; only the force is reduced.
**What is not gained.** Work ✓ Pushing at 0·4 m needs four times the force but the
point moves through a quarter of the distance for the same door rotation, so
W = Fd is unchanged. A lever multiplies force, never energy.
**A check in terms of angle.** Opening the door through 1 radian moves the far edge
1·6 m and the near point 0·4 m:
work = 1 x 1·6 = **1·6 J** in both cases ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **1·2 N** ✗ and **2·4 N** ✗ are too small - the force must
**increase** when the arm shortens. **3·6 N** ✗ is a near miss, corresponding to
d = 0·44 m ✓
∴ 4 N.

When any wave crosses into a new medium, the **frequency** is the one thing that does
**not** change.
**Step 1 — see why the frequency is fixed.** It is set by the **source** ✓ The boundary
cannot create or destroy wave crests, so crests must leave the interface at exactly the
rate they arrive. The frequency is therefore the same in both media - and the first
statement is the one that does **not** hold.
**Step 2 — check the other three.**
"**the speed changes**" ✓ **true** - v = c/n, so radiation slows in a denser medium
"**they travel in straight lines in a given medium**" ✓ **true** - thermal radiation is
electromagnetic and travels rectilinearly in a homogeneous medium
"**the wavelength changes**" ✓ **true** - with f fixed and v changing, λ = v/f must
change
**Step 3 — conclude.** The statement about **frequency** changing is the false one ✓
**The relation that ties them together.**
v = fλ ✓
f is fixed by the source, v by the medium, so λ must adjust. In glass of n = 1·5, both
the speed and the wavelength fall to **two thirds** of their vacuum values.
**Why colour is unchanged under water.** Perceived colour follows the **frequency**,
not the wavelength ✓ A diver sees objects in their proper colours even though every
wavelength has shrunk by a factor of 4/3.
**The photon argument.** A photon's energy is **E = hf** ✓ If f changed at a boundary,
energy would be created or destroyed there - which nothing in the interaction permits.
**What thermal radiation actually is.** Electromagnetic waves, mostly **infrared** for
bodies near room temperature ✓ obeying exactly the same laws of reflection, refraction
and interference as visible light.
**The one case where frequency does change.** When the source or observer **moves** -
the **Doppler effect** ✓ But that is a change in the source-observer relationship, not
something the medium does.
**Why this question is worth asking.** The instinct is that "everything changes" at a
boundary ✓ Fixing firmly that **frequency is the invariant** resolves most confusions
in refraction problems.
∴ the statement that the frequency changes when it travels from one medium to another.
